The early life history of the Iceland cockle (Ciliatocardium ciliatum) begins with a fertilised egg of an estimated diameter of 65 micrometres, which yields a calculated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000000144 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000000144 grams]. Following a brief planktotrophic larval phase, the veliger larva undergoes metamorphosis and settlement onto the seabed at a remarkably small shell length of just 0.2 centimetres . This metamorphic transition marks the onset of the post-metamorphic juvenile stage, during which the young spat begin filtering phytoplankton from the surrounding water column. The prodissoconch formed during the larval phase gives way to the juvenile dissoconch as shell secretion accelerates. Growth during this early benthic period is heavily influenced by local food availability and substrate type, with individuals in coarse, organically rich sediments often progressing faster than those on bare sand. The species is common in subarctic and boreal waters of the North Atlantic, where it occupies depths ranging from the intertidal zone down to approximately 100 metres, often burrowing just beneath the sediment surface.

As juveniles continue to develop, they eventually reach the shell length at which sexual maturation is initiated. For the Iceland cockle, the transition from the juvenile to the reproductively active adult stage, which we may approximate using values documented in the closely related common cockle Cerastoderma edule, occurs when the shell attains a length of 1.2 centimetres [Lp = 1.2 centimetres]. At this threshold, gonad maturation begins, and the energy budget of the growing mollusc shifts progressively from an exclusive focus on somatic increase toward the production of gametes. The period leading up to this milestone is characterised by rapid allometric growth, with the shell increasing in both length and thickness. Environmental conditions such as temperature and food supply strongly modulate the timing of this transition, with individuals in colder, less productive waters potentially experiencing a delay in reaching this crucial developmental benchmark compared with those in more favourable habitats. The onset of gametogenesis is a pivotal event in the life cycle, as it marks the point at which the individual transitions from a strictly feeding, growing juvenile to an organism capable of contributing to the next generation.

Once sexual maturity has been attained, the reproductively active adult Iceland cockle invests significantly in reproductive output. Under the sustained cold conditions typical of its subarctic habitat, specifically at a water temperature of 3 °C [T = 3 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate has been estimated at 4657 gametes per day [Ri = 4657 gametes per day]. This high fecundity is characteristic of many bivalve species that broadcast their gametes into the water column, relying on external fertilisation and a planktonic larval phase to disperse offspring over wide areas. The production of such a large number of eggs represents a substantial energetic investment for the female, requiring the mobilisation of reserves accumulated during the preceding feeding season. Spawning events are typically synchronised with the local spring phytoplankton bloom, ensuring that newly released larvae have an abundant supply of food during their early planktotrophic development. The timing and magnitude of spawning can vary considerably from year to year, closely tracking interannual fluctuations in primary productivity and water temperature. These dense spawning events often result in a brief but intense pulse of gametes entering the water column.

Throughout its adult life, the Iceland cockle continues to grow, albeit at a decelerating rate as it approaches its maximum size. The ultimate shell length attained by this species is approximately 4.5 centimetres [Li = approximately 4.5 centimetres], a modest size that places it among the smaller members of the cockle family in its region. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight achieved by a fully grown adult is around 11.3 grams [Wwi = around 11.3 grams], reflecting the associated increase in soft-tissue mass and shell material. This asymptotic size is not reached uniformly across all populations; local conditions such as sediment grain size, food supply, and population density can produce notable variation in mean adult size. Growth rates are generally highest during the first few years of benthic life and then slow considerably as the animal ages, with increments in shell length becoming barely perceptible in the oldest individuals. The pattern of growth is well described by a decelerating curve typical of many iteroparous marine invertebrates that continue to invest in reproduction throughout their long adult lives. This allocation strategy, favouring sustained but moderate annual fecundity over a single massive reproductive event, appears well suited to the relatively stable but unproductive environments the species inhabits.

The lifespan of the Iceland cockle is closely tied to the cold thermal regime of its environment. Under the same low temperature conditions that govern its reproductive rate, specifically at 3 °C [T = 3 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan extends to approximately 8760 days [am = approximately 8760 days], which is equivalent to about 24 years. This extraordinary longevity is among the highest documented for bivalves of comparable adult body size and reflects the profoundly slowed metabolic and physiological processes that occur at near-freezing temperatures. Senescence in this species is gradual, with no abrupt post-reproductive decline; individuals continue to spawn each year well into their third decade of life. Natural mortality factors include predation by demersal fishes, such as cod and flatfish, as well as sea stars and large gastropods that are capable of prying open the shell. The thick, ribbed valves provide substantial mechanical protection against many predators, but they are not impervious to the crushing jaws of large decapod crustaceans. The species' long life and sustained fecundity represent a classic bet-hedging strategy, ensuring that even in years of poor recruitment, enough reproductive events occur over an individual's lifetime to maintain the population.
